---
title: "014 — Settings page navigation"
---

> **Status:** standing

**Goal.** Make any section of the single, long `/settings` page reachable in one
interaction. The reported pain was concrete: finding Backup meant scrolling past
everything above it — and Backup sits second-from-bottom. The feature keeps the page
exactly as it is, one route with sections in their current order, and adds navigation
around it: a sticky anchor rail mirroring the real headings with a scroll-spy highlight;
a visible search field (cmd-K as enhancement, scoped to settings) over a static section
index with aliases; URL hash anchors with strict history discipline; and a mobile
floating jump button opening a compact sheet. The success bar: a known section reached
in a single click with zero scrolling, under three seconds by name, the highlight
correct in 100% of spot checks even after content-height changes, no history entries
from scrolling, no unsaved edit ever lost to a jump, and any section within two taps on
a phone.

**Why.** The idea stage (`ideas/001-settings-navigation`, condensed with this feature)
had already played the deck and its verdict assembled a composite rather than picking a
card: keep the single page — the shrink-the-page and routed-subpages bets declined,
because subpages' URL powers could be captured by hash sync without route surgery, and
only a never-unmounting page dodges the unsaved-changes trilemma — with the sticky rail
as the spine, search absorbed into it, and mobile left explicitly open for the spec to
decide (it became a floating button plus bottom sheet). The frustration was scan-load
on a known-target hunt, a navigation problem rather than an organization problem, so
reorganizing sections was ruled out by the verdict itself.

**Outcome & reversals.** Specced, built, and merged the same day (August 28). Research
corrected the spec's own assumption before implementation: three listed sections turned
out to be eight, verified against the DOM, and the inventory froze into a static
registry whose labels are pinned by tests. The build split cleanly — pure modules
(registry; hash-sync with push-on-jump, replace-on-spy, and duplicate suppression; an
IntersectionObserver scroll-spy with a pure reducer and no scroll listeners) plus
presentation-only components and one shared jump pipeline: push, smooth-scroll, heading
flash, optimistic highlight, hash frozen while a jump scroll is in flight. Research
also caught that `window` never scrolls in the app shell — spy and scroll code must
target `<main>`, or silently no-op. cmd-K was scoped to settings so the global
`/search` binding survived untouched. Perf was measured before and after under a
dedicated probe scenario, an accessibility pass covered rail, sheet, and flash, and all
26 tasks closed. The maintenance design then proved itself: the public-launch security
panels and [017 — section peek strip](017-section-peek-strip.qmd)'s new Chat section —
whose aliases literally read "strip, outline" — joined the page later by editing the
one registry, no component changes. No later feature has overturned any of its
contracts.

**Learnings.**

- Navigation chrome that mirrors real structure beats reorganizing: freezing content
  and adding a map around it fixed findability without touching a section.
- A static, test-pinned index beats DOM scraping — labels cannot silently drift, and
  new sections join by editing one registry.
- History discipline is a state machine, not styling: push only explicit jumps, replace
  spy updates, suppress duplicates, or Back becomes a scrolling slideshow.
- In a shell layout, target the real scroll container; window-level scroll code fails
  silently.
